rationale: The student must decide to introduce an auxiliary parallel through the bend, connect the reflex angle and transferred 40° to the remaining angle, and use a supplementary-angle converse to establish parallelism. The construction and proof are unsignposted, but rely on familiar angle facts; the prompt already states the conclusion and does not require reasons.
scopeRationale: The retained practice context uses reflex angles and parallel-angle transfers (3e–h), co-interior angles (4d), their converse in a proof (18), and alternate-angle transfer in a proof (19). Drawing an auxiliary parallel is a non-routine connection of these prior facts, not a later-topic dependency.
sourceFidelity: The full source prompt and all five point labels, segments, numerical angles and reflex sector are retained. Source mark allocation is omitted under the current convention; black 10 pt typography and line styling are house adaptations. Worked text preserves the complete source solution; the short answer compresses the same method. The solution-only auxiliary line and computed angles add source-solution information without leaking it into the question.
derivation: At B, BA has direction 10° and BC −30°, so angle ABC is 40°. At D, DC points 90° and DE 190°, giving angle CDE 100°. At C, CD points 270° and CB 150°; the code's counterclockwise arc from 270° to 510° is the 240° reflex sector, leaving 120°. Construct CF in direction 190°, parallel to AB. CB points 150°, so angle FCB is 40° by alternate angles, and angle FCD is 120°−40°=80°. With transversal CD, angles FCD and CDE are co-interior and sum to 180°, so CF is parallel to DE; because CF is also parallel to AB, AB is parallel to DE. The native solution diagram's arcs B–C–F and F–C–D represent 40° and 80° respectively, and both short and worked answers give this chain. The proof derives the stated relationship from the numerical givens and construction without using the desired parallelism as a premise.
